484.title: Daughters of Jerusalem (Luke 23:27–31)
484.hook: on the road he turns to the weeping women
484.howItsDone: Many Catholics pray the Stations of the Cross on the Fridays of Lent, walking from one image to the next around the church; the eighth station is Jesus meeting the women of Jerusalem.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Herod's mockery: a ruler who wanted a show and got nothing. Your line was silence before herod. Where did you skip a performance? Day four hundred eighty-four, and a new week on the road to the cross.

On the wall of a parish church, the eighth of the traditional Stations of the Cross: Jesus meets the women of Jerusalem. Often it's a carved panel, a bent figure with the cross and a few women with their hands to their faces. The scene comes from Luke alone. The sentence has been passed. Jesus is being led away, and the soldiers have seized a man named Simon of Cyrene, coming in from the country, to carry the cross behind him. A great crowd follows, and among them women who bewail and lament him. Today he stops, and turns, and speaks to them.
screen: `THE EIGHTH STATION.` → `SIMON CARRIES THE CROSS.` → `WOMEN MOURNING ON THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Here's what he says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Daughters of Jerusalem, weep not over me; but weep for yourselves, and for your children." It's a startling thing to hear from a man on his way to be crucified. Someone else has been made to carry his cross. And his attention goes outward, to the people beside the road and to what is coming for their city. Luke has prepared us for this. A few chapters back, Jesus wept over Jerusalem as he rode toward it. Now he turns the women's tears in the same direction. He speaks of days when people will call the childless blessed, and will ask the mountains to fall on them. And then a proverb readers still turn over: "For if in the green wood they do these things, what shall be done in the dry?" Green wood doesn't catch easily. Dry wood does. One common reading goes like this: if they do this to the innocent one, what will happen when the times get truly dry and hard? Some readers connect his warning with the later Roman destruction of Jerusalem. Notice what he doesn't do. He doesn't brush the women off. He doesn't say their tears are wrong. He takes them seriously enough to answer them, and to point their grief at the people they love. The scene became a station on the Way of the Cross, and it shows something hard to fake: in the middle of his own suffering, he still sees the people in front of him.
screen: `WEEP NOT OVER ME.` · `WEEP FOR YOUR CHILDREN.` · `GREEN WOOD AND DRY.` · `HE STILL SEES THEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice others while you suffer. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind whatever is heavy for you right now. Don't push it away; let it be there. Then, gently, look past it. Who is near you this week? A coworker who seems tired. A kid who has been quiet. A parent on the phone who changed the subject. Pick one face. Hold it next to your own trouble, not instead of it. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. If you don't, just decide one small way to notice them today. The bell holds the time.
Daughters of Jerusalem. The women who mourned Jesus on the road, and whom he turned to and answered, the eighth Station of the Cross. Today's word.
Your line: weep for yourselves. Today, on a heavy day, look up once and ask someone else how they're really doing. Day four hundred eighty-four.

this scene is told only in Luke.
Jesus told the women their tears were wrong
he turned them: weep not over me, but weep for yourselves and your children.
meeting the women is one of the Stations of the Cross
it's the eighth station in the traditional Way of the Cross.

fork.setup: you're being led out to be crucified. a stranger has been made to carry your cross. women by the road are crying out for you. what do you do?
options: keep walking; you have nothing left to give.
turn and speak to them about their children.
ask them to help carry the cross.
fork.reveal: he turns: "Daughters of Jerusalem, weep not over me; but weep for yourselves, and for your children." even now his attention goes outward.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus scolds the women for crying.
what it means: he takes their grief seriously and points it at the people they love and what's coming for the city.
what a scholar hears: the green and dry wood proverb is obscure; some readers connect the warning with Rome's later destruction of Jerusalem.

485.title: Father, forgive them (Luke 23:34)
485.hook: for they know not what they do
485.howItsDone: Catholics hear Luke 23:34 in the Passion on Palm Sunday in the year of Luke, and some parishes keep a Good Friday devotion on the Seven Last Words, of which this is counted the first.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the daughters of Jerusalem: on the road, he turned to the women and answered their tears. Your line was weep for yourselves. Whose day did you notice, even on a heavy one? Day four hundred eighty-five.

The place is called Calvary, the skull. Two criminals are led out with him, one on his right and one on his left. Luke tells it almost without detail. They crucified him there. No description of nails, no long account of pain. Soon the soldiers will be casting lots for his clothes. And into that ordinary cruelty, the first thing Luke has Jesus say from the cross is not a cry of pain and not a curse. It's a prayer, and it begins with today's word.
screen: `A PLACE CALLED CALVARY.` → `TWO CRIMINALS, ONE EACH SIDE.` → `THE FIRST WORD FROM THE CROSS.`

segments.voice: In the Douay-Rheims: "And Jesus said: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do." Start with the first word. Father. Jesus has called God Father all through Luke: at twelve in the temple, I must be about my Father's business; in the garden, Father, if thou wilt. Now, nailed to wood, he still prays the same way. The relationship holds, even here. Then the request. Forgive them. Who is them? Luke doesn't say. The soldiers, surely, who are doing the nailing. Some readers widen it to everyone who brought him here. And then the reason: they know not what they do. Not that it's fine. Not that it doesn't matter. Only that they don't fully see what they're doing. Catholic devotion counts this as the first of the Seven Last Words, sayings of Jesus from the cross gathered from all four Gospels, and some parishes keep a Good Friday devotion that preaches on them one by one. And Luke shows the prayer didn't end at the cross. In his second book, Acts, the deacon Stephen, dying under stones, prays nearly the same prayer for the people throwing them. It's the hardest forgiveness there is, the kind given while the hurt is still happening.
screen: `FATHER, EVEN HERE.` · `FORGIVE THEM: WHO IS THEM?` · `THE FIRST OF SEVEN LAST WORDS.` · `STEPHEN PRAYS IT TOO.` · then, large: `FOR THEY KNOW NOT WHAT THEY DO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: forgive someone who doesn't know. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who hurt you without understanding it. A parent who said the wrong thing. A friend who never noticed what they missed. A stranger who was careless. They may never know. Hold them in mind and try the words they know not. It doesn't excuse what happened, and it doesn't mean you have to go back. If you pray, you can use the prayer from the cross for them. If not, just loosen your grip a little. The bell holds the time.
Father. The first word of the first saying from the cross in Luke: Father, forgive them. In Greek, pater. Today's word.
Your line: they know not. Today, when someone hurts you without seeing it, say it once to yourself before you answer. Day four hundred eighty-five.

options: a curse on the men doing it.
a cry to be taken down.

fork.reveal: "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do." the first word from the cross in Luke is a prayer for the people causing the pain.

original.note: Greek: Father, the first word of the prayer from the cross in Luke 23:34.

trapdoor: what you thought: forgiveness means saying it didn't matter.
what it means: Jesus asks forgiveness for people who don't see what they're doing, while they're still doing it.
what a scholar hears: Luke never says who them is, and in Acts 7:60 he has Stephen, dying, echo the same prayer.

486.title: The centurion glorifies God (Luke 23:44–49)
486.hook: Indeed this was a just man, and the crowds go home beating their breasts
486.howItsDone: Catholics hear Luke's account of the death in the Palm Sunday Passion in the year of Luke, and pray "into thy hands" from Psalm 31 each night at Compline; at Mass they strike the breast during the Confiteor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first word from the cross: Father, forgive them. Your line was they know not. Did you get to say it once, quietly, before you answered someone? Day four hundred eighty-six.

At every Mass, near the start, Catholics say the Confiteor, the I confess. At the words through my fault, the missal has the people strike their breast. It's a small, old gesture: a closed hand to the chest. Where does it come from? One place it shows up is today's reading. It's about the sixth hour, around noon, on the day of the crucifixion, and darkness comes over the whole earth until the ninth hour. The veil of the temple is torn down the middle. Jesus cries out with a loud voice, and dies. And then Luke turns the camera away from the cross, to the people standing in front of it.
screen: `A HAND TO THE CHEST AT MASS.` → `DARKNESS AT THE SIXTH HOUR.` → `THE CAMERA TURNS TO THE CROWD.`

segments.voice: Luke's Jesus dies with a psalm on his lips. In the Douay-Rheims: "Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit." It's a line from Psalm thirty, thirty-one in other Bibles, a prayer of trust, and the Church prays it at Compline, its prayer before sleep. Then Luke shows us three reactions. First, the soldier in charge of the execution. A centurion, a Roman officer, who has watched the whole thing up close. "Now the centurion, seeing what was done, glorified God, saying: Indeed this was a just man." Matthew and Mark have him say this was the Son of God. Luke has a just man, innocent, righteous, and frames it as praise. The first reaction Luke reports after the death is a Roman officer glorifying God. Second, the crowds. They came, Luke says, to see a spectacle. They go home striking their breasts. No speech. Just a gesture of grief and something like guilt, carried home down the road. Third, his friends. All his acquaintances, and the women who had followed him from Galilee, stood afar off, watching. They don't leave. They can't do anything. They stay. These three are a map of how people stand at the cross. Some see clearly and say so. Some feel it in the chest and go home changed. And some simply refuse to look away. Catholic devotion has a name for the last kind, from the old hymn Stabat Mater: the mother standing. Luke doesn't name Mary here; John does. But the women from Galilee are there, and that matters. The women who watch him die are the women who will go to the tomb.
screen: `INTO THY HANDS.` · `A SOLDIER SAYS: A JUST MAN.` · `THE CROWD STRIKES THEIR BREASTS.` · `THE WOMEN STAND AFAR OFF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stay a moment at the cross. Settle, and breathe. If there's a crucifix near you, look at it. If not, picture one, or simply picture that hill in the afternoon dark. Don't try to feel anything in particular. Just stay, the way the women stayed, afar off and watching. When your mind wanders, come back to the picture. If you pray, you can say his last line from the psalm, into thy hands. If you don't, just keep your attention there. The bell holds the time.
The centurion glorifies God. A Roman officer at the cross who, when Jesus died, glorified God, saying: indeed this was a just man. Today's word.
Your line: a just man. Today, say out loud one true, good thing about someone who isn't in the room to hear it. Day four hundred eighty-six.

fork.reveal: he glorified God, saying: indeed this was a just man. the first response Luke reports to the death is praise, from the soldier in charge.

original.note: Greek: just, righteous, innocent, what the centurion calls Jesus in Luke 23:47.

trapdoor: what you thought: the centurion was a random bystander.
what it means: the officer at the execution glorifies God as Jesus dies.
what a scholar hears: Luke's dikaios (just, innocent) where Matthew and Mark have Son of God; it fits Luke's steady theme that Jesus was innocent.

487.title: Idle tales (Luke 23:55–24:12)
487.hook: the women tell the apostles, and the words seem like idle tales
487.howItsDone: Catholics hear Luke's account of the empty tomb at the Easter Vigil in the year of Luke, the night the Alleluia returns after Lent.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the centurion at the cross: indeed, a just man. Your line was a just man. Who did you speak well of when they weren't around? Day four hundred eighty-seven.

Friday evening. The women from Galilee follow the body to the tomb and watch exactly where it's laid. Then they go home and prepare spices and ointments. The Sabbath begins, and Luke says they rested, according to the commandment. Saturday is a long, silent day. Very early on Sunday, in the half dark, they walk back carrying the spices. They've come to do the last thing love can do for the dead. The stone is rolled back. The body is gone. And two men in shining clothes are standing there. Today, the first people to hear the news, and the first people not to be believed.
screen: `THEY WATCH WHERE HE IS LAID.` → `A SILENT SABBATH.` → `SPICES AT DAWN, AN EMPTY TOMB.`

segments.voice: The two men ask the question that turns the whole Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "Why seek you the living with the dead? He is not here, but is risen." And then: remember. Remember what he told you in Galilee. Luke says simply: and they remembered his words. So the women go back and tell the eleven and all the rest. Luke names them: Mary Magdalen, Joanna, Mary the mother of James, and other women with them. And here's how the news lands: "And these words seemed to them as idle tales; and they did not believe them." Idle tales. The Greek word is leros, and it's blunt. Nonsense. Silly talk. It's a word a medical writer of the time might use for the babbling of someone in a fever. The apostles, the men chosen and trained for three years, hear the first announcement of the resurrection and call it nonsense. Luke doesn't hide it. He could have. Peter does get up and run to the tomb. He stoops down, sees the linen cloths lying there by themselves, and goes home wondering. Not believing yet. Wondering. Notice what the women had to go on. Not a body. Not proof. An empty space, two strangers, and a memory: they remembered his words. Earlier in Luke, when Jesus told the twelve what would happen in Jerusalem, they understood none of it. Now the women carry those same words back to them. The first people sent to say he is risen are the ones who came at dawn to anoint a corpse.
screen: `WHY SEEK THE LIVING WITH THE DEAD?` · `THE WOMEN REMEMBER, AND TELL.` · `LEROS: IT SOUNDED LIKE NONSENSE.` · `PETER RUNS, AND WONDERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: believe someone's good news. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who told you something good lately and got a shrug back. A kid's story about their day. A friend who said things are finally getting better. A coworker excited about an idea you assumed wouldn't work. Picture their face as they told you. Now hear it again, and this time let it be true. Let yourself be glad with them. If you pray, you can thank God for their news. The bell holds the time.
Idle tales. What the apostles called the women's report of the empty tomb. In Greek, leros: nonsense. They were wrong. Today's word.
Your line: not idle tales. Today, when someone brings you good news, ask them one more question about it instead of doubting it. Day four hundred eighty-seven.

trapdoor: what you thought: the apostles were the first to hear the resurrection.
what it means: the women heard first, remembered, and told, and the men dismissed it.
what a scholar hears: leros appears only here in the New Testament; Luke keeps an unflattering detail about the apostles in plain view.

488.title: Emmaus, slowly (Luke 24:13–35)
488.hook: stay with us, because it is towards evening
488.howItsDone: Catholics hear the Emmaus story in Easter week and on the Third Sunday of Easter in one year of the cycle, and Catholic teaching points to it as the pattern of the Mass: the Liturgy of the Word, then the Liturgy of the Eucharist.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the women at the tomb, and the apostles who heard it as idle tales. Your line was not idle tales. Whose good news did you let be true? Day four hundred eighty-eight.

The same Sunday, in the afternoon. Two disciples are walking away from Jerusalem, toward a village called Emmaus, about sixty furlongs off, seven miles or so. One is named Cleophas. The other Luke never names. They're talking about everything that has happened, the way people talk after a funeral, going over it and over it. A stranger falls into step with them and asks what they're discussing. They stop, faces sad. Are you the only visitor in Jerusalem who doesn't know? Today we walk the road to Emmaus, slowly, because Luke tells it slowly, and the slowness is the point.
screen: `TWO WALKING AWAY.` → `A STRANGER FALLS INTO STEP.` → `ARE YOU THE ONLY ONE WHO DOESN'T KNOW?`

segments.voice: They tell him the whole story, and the line that carries their grief is in the past tense: we hoped that it was he that should have redeemed Israel. We hoped. The stranger answers by walking them through the scriptures, beginning with Moses and all the prophets, showing what they said about the Christ. It takes miles. Then they reach the village, and he makes as if to keep going. And they won't let him. In the Douay-Rheims: "But they constrained him; saying: Stay with us, because it is towards evening, and the day is now far spent. And he went in with them." At table he takes bread, blesses it, breaks it, and gives it to them. "And their eyes were opened, and they knew him: and he vanished out of their sight." Afterward they say their hearts were burning while he opened the scriptures on the road, and that same hour they go back to Jerusalem to tell the others how he was known to them in the breaking of bread. Catholic teaching sees the shape of the Mass in this story. First the word: the scriptures opened and explained. Then the table: bread taken, blessed, broken, given. Saint John Paul the Second built his letter for the Year of the Eucharist around this scene and titled it with the disciples' plea in Latin, Mane nobiscum Domine, stay with us, Lord. Notice, too, what doesn't happen. He doesn't force his way in. He would have walked on. The invitation is theirs. Luke shows the risen Christ waiting to be asked.
screen: `WE HOPED.` · `THE SCRIPTURES OPENED ON THE ROAD.` · `STAY WITH US, IT IS TOWARDS EVENING.` · `KNOWN IN THE BREAKING OF BREAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: invite Christ to stay tonight. Settle, and breathe. Think back over today as if it were a road. Where were you walking, and what were you talking about? What did you hope for that didn't happen? Let it be there, the way it was for those two. Then picture the evening coming in, the light going. If you pray, you can use their words: stay with us, because it is towards evening. If you don't, just notice what you would want to stay with you tonight. The bell holds the time.
Emmaus. The village seven miles from Jerusalem where two disciples knew the risen Jesus in the breaking of bread. Nobody is certain where it was. Today's word.
Your line: stay with us. Today, at dinner, notice who is at your table, and make one of them welcome to stay a little longer. Day four hundred eighty-eight.

John Paul II named a letter after their plea

options: thank him and say goodbye.
beg him to stay with you.
ask his name before he goes.
fork.reveal: they constrained him: stay with us, because it is towards evening. he went in, broke the bread, and they knew him.

original.note: Latin, from the Vulgate of Luke 24:29: stay with us. John Paul II's 2004 letter takes its title from it.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about two people who didn't recognize a friend.
what it means: the risen Christ is known when the scriptures are opened and the bread is broken, and he waits to be invited.
what a scholar hears: the four table verbs (took, blessed, broke, gave) echo the Last Supper; Emmaus's location is still debated.

489.title: Handle and see (Luke 24:36–43)
489.hook: he shows his hands and feet and eats a piece of broiled fish
489.howItsDone: Catholics hear Luke 24:35–48 on the Third Sunday of Easter in Year B of the Sunday cycle, and profess "the resurrection of the body" in the Apostles' Creed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the road to Emmaus, and two people who begged a stranger to stay with us. Who did you make welcome at your table? Day four hundred eighty-nine.

A room in Jerusalem, that same Sunday evening. The two from Emmaus have just burst in, out of breath, telling how they knew him in the breaking of bread. Everyone is talking at once. And then, while they're still speaking, he is standing in the middle of them. Peace be to you. Nobody cheers. Luke says they were troubled and frightened, and thought they were seeing a spirit. A ghost. Today Jesus answers their fear plainly, with his hands and with a piece of fish.
screen: `THE EMMAUS TWO BURST IN.` → `HE STANDS IN THE MIDDLE.` → `THEY THINK IT'S A GHOST.`

segments.voice: He asks why they're troubled, and then he offers himself. In the Douay-Rheims: "See my hands and feet, that it is I myself; handle, and see: for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as you see me to have." Handle, and see. Touch me. The Greek verb means to feel with the hands, the way you'd feel for a light switch in the dark. And still, Luke says, they didn't believe, for joy. Isn't that an honest line? Too happy to believe it. So he asks a very ordinary question: have you anything here to eat? "And they offered him a piece of a broiled fish, and a honeycomb." And he took it, and ate it in front of them. A ghost doesn't eat fish. That's the whole argument, and it's a kitchen-table argument. Luke cares about bodies all the way through: a baby in a manger, a woman bent double, a servant's ear. He won't let the resurrection drift into a feeling or a memory. The Catechism says the same thing in its own way: the risen Jesus is not a ghost; he invites touch and shares a meal, and his body is truly his own, the one that was crucified, though now in a new, glorified state. That's why Catholics say in the Creed that they believe in the resurrection of the body. Not escaping the body. The body, raised. He shows them his hands and feet on purpose.
screen: `TROUBLED: IT MUST BE A SPIRIT.` · `HANDLE, AND SEE.` · `THEY DISBELIEVED FOR JOY.` · `A PIECE OF BROILED FISH.` · then, large: `THE RESURRECTION OF THE BODY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: eat something as a sign of life. If you have something small nearby, a bite of bread, a piece of fruit, even a glass of water, take it. If not, just picture your next meal. Settle, and breathe. Eat slowly. Notice the weight in your hand, the taste, the swallow. This body is alive, and it gets hungry, and that's not beneath faith. If you pray, you can give thanks for being alive in a body. If you don't, just let the plain fact of eating be enough. The bell holds the time.
Handle and see. The risen Jesus inviting his frightened friends to touch his hands and feet: a spirit hath not flesh and bones. Today's word.
Your line: a ghost doesn't eat fish. Today, at one meal, put the phone down and eat like it matters that you have a body. Day four hundred eighty-nine.

what it means: in Luke, the risen Jesus can be touched and eats fish. the same body, raised.

490.title: He opened their understanding (Luke 24:44–49)
490.hook: the whole of the scriptures is about him
490.howItsDone: Catholics hear the scriptures at Mass in a pattern that pairs an Old Testament reading with the Gospel, and the Church teaches, in Dei Verbum, that the two Testaments are read in the light of each other.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the frightened room: handle and see, and a piece of broiled fish. Your line was a ghost doesn't eat fish. Did you eat one meal like your body mattered? Day four hundred ninety.

Some books only make sense on the second read. The detective novel where the last chapter sends you back to page one, and suddenly every small detail was a clue. The film you rewatch knowing the twist, and now the opening scene means something else. The disciples have had the scriptures all their lives. Moses, the prophets, the psalms, read aloud every Sabbath since they were children. They know the words. But tonight, still in that room, with the fish bones on the table, the risen Jesus gives them the last chapter, and sends them back to page one.
screen: `SOME BOOKS NEED A SECOND READ.` → `THEY KNOW THE WORDS ALREADY.` → `NOW, THE LAST CHAPTER.`

segments.voice: He reminds them that he told them all this while he was still with them: everything written about him in the law of Moses, in the prophets, and in the psalms had to be fulfilled. Those are the three parts of the scriptures as people in his time often named them, so he is saying: the whole book. Then the sentence that gives today its name, in the Douay-Rheims: "Then he opened their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures." Opened. It's the same Greek verb Luke has been using all chapter. On the road, the scriptures were opened to the two from Emmaus. At the table, their eyes were opened. Now, minds are opened. Luke is telling us that reading the Bible well isn't only a matter of effort. Something has to be opened, and the risen Christ is the one who opens it. He sums it up: the Christ should suffer, and rise again the third day, and repentance and forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name to all nations, beginning at Jerusalem. You are witnesses, he tells them. And then: stay in the city until you are clothed with power from on high. A promise Luke will keep in his second book, Acts, at Pentecost. The Catholic Church reads the scriptures this way to this day. The Second Vatican Council, in Dei Verbum, says the two Testaments belong together, and quotes an old line from Saint Augustine: the New is hidden in the Old, and the Old is made plain in the New. Catholics also say the Old Testament keeps its own lasting worth, and the Jewish people read these same books in their own living tradition. Both are true at once.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask to understand one passage. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a line of scripture that has always puzzled you, or bothered you, or just slid past. Maybe one from this week: green wood and dry, or forgive them, or the idle tales. Hold it in mind without trying to solve it. Turn it over slowly. If you pray, you can ask simply to understand it. If you don't, just stay curious with it, the way you'd sit with a hard question from a friend. The bell holds the time.
He opened their understanding. The risen Jesus showing his disciples that the law, the prophets and the psalms speak of him. Today's word.
